normalize/batch: Batch normalization looks at one feature at a time, across every example in the batch. Here is one feature over a batch of four: nine, three, seventeen and eleven.
normalize/mean: First, the batch mean, written with the Greek letter mu. They add up to forty, so mu is ten.
normalize/var: Then the variance: the average squared distance from the mean. One, forty nine, forty nine and one average to twenty five. Its square root, the square root of twenty five, is five: the standard deviation. Here sigma means this spread, not the sigmoid, so the variance is sigma squared.
normalize/xhat: Subtract the mean, and divide by the standard deviation. The result is x hat, the normalized x: x hat is x minus mu, over sigma. Nine becomes minus zero point two, and three becomes minus one point four.
normalize/eps: The formula adds a tiny epsilon to the variance, so it never divides by zero. For arithmetic by hand, it can be ignored.
normalize/unit: Now the feature has mean zero and variance one, whatever scale it arrived at.
affine/gamma: Forcing mean zero and variance one every time could be too rigid. So batch norm adds two learned numbers per feature: a scale, gamma, and a shift, beta. The output is y equals gamma x hat, plus beta.
affine/y: With gamma two and beta one, minus zero point two becomes two times minus zero point two, plus one: zero point six.
affine/undo: If the network learns gamma equal to the standard deviation and beta equal to the mean, it undoes the normalization entirely. It gets to choose.
test/running: During training, every batch has its own mean and variance, and batch norm keeps running averages of both.
test/test: At test time it normalizes with those running averages, not with the test batch. So an example's output never depends on which other examples came with it.
